Mr. Speaker, since I shall not be a member of this committee I desire to make one or two remarks. Like the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) I was surprised that the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) did not make some reference to the matter of Annapolis-Kings and the result there under the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. I want to endorse what the member for Lake Centre said about that and to a quote a little further from the report, which is to be found on page 83 of Votes and Proceedings. Section 6 reads:
The evidence indicates a disorganized polling booth where a considerable number of persons were walking around. The officer seems to have considered that he had no duty in regard to anything except signing the certificates.
According to reports I have heard this section could apply to many training centres across Canada. Section 7 reads:
Under order of headquarters, the commissioned officer made no inquiry of voters. He interpreted his instructions to mean that if a declaration was presented to him and signed, he would certify it and give a ballot to the person presenting it, even if he knew that that person was not entitled to vote.
That is a pretty glaring statement, Mr. Speaker. I can tell you that many personnel in large training centres in western Canada were amazed at the type of campaign carried on, and at matters pertaining to taking the vote in these centres. I hope that this matter will be gone into by this committee, and that the election act will be so amended that we will be sure that there will not be a repetition of this sort of thing in the future, because it has been very bad business.
The point I do want to make is this. It may be a bit of a fetish with me. It has been referred to by other speakers today. Ever since coming to this parliament I have been concerned about the matter of the transferable vote. It has been pretty well covered today. I want to add that in this present House of Commons we have at least 121 members who have been elected by a minority of the votes cast in their respective constituencies. I know it was surprising to many people to find that, according to the chief electoral officer's figures, the majority of those citizens in Canada who cast their votes on June 27 last year did not vote for this government.

My hon. friend can laugh and chuckle as he likes, but it does not affect me one iota. If he is able enough to rise in his place and contradict that statement then he may laugh to his heart's desire, but I am making the statement that, according to the figures released by the chief electoral officer, the majority of the electors casting their votes on June 27 did not vote for this government. That does not reflect anything on the government. It is due to our election act. I am neither admitting nor disputing the fact that they have probably 75 members in this House of Commons who were elected with a minority vote cast on that day. I am not predicting what might happen at another election. The same thing could happen, or it might be reversed. The point I want to make is this. In a democracy I think that before a person is declared elected he should, on the transfer of votes, have received a majority of the votes cast in the riding. I have put the figures on record in the speech from the throne debate. They may be found at pages 110 and 111 of Hansard. I do not want to repeat them at this time. The figures with respect to the last general election in this country can be checked.
As I say, not being a member of the committee I would sincerely hope that they will give serious consideration to the matter of the transferable vote and of providing for it under the Dominion Elections Act, 1938. I can say that I know something of the manner in which it has worked in Manitoba. I cannot tell you how many years it has been in force there, but it has been in force in quite a number of general provincial elections in that province, and I believe also in Alberta.
I simply repeat, Mr. Speaker, I am sincere in asking that the committee give the most serious consideration to amending the Dominion Elections Act and making provision for the transferable vote at any future elections.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the January 21, 1950, issue of the Saturday Evening Post, Mr. David G. Wittels who had made a survey of the situation in the United States, describes divorce as "our biggest national scandal" and later told in a series of articles "the sordid story of America's broken homes".
Considering the present sad trends, the same thing will soon apply to Canada.
The philosophy of those who would make divorce easier no doubt finds justification in their minds because of their particular beliefs. May I tell them that I fail to grasp their point of view and that their arguments, based on false principles, can in no way change the attitude I have at all times defended in this house regarding this matter of national importance.
The principle of the indissolubility of marriage must be upheld with the utmost vigour and any attempt at compromise must be rejected. Adultery having been recognized as grounds for divorce, it is logical that it should be resorted to by those seeking divorce. That is the unfortunate situation with which we are faced in this country today.
In requesting the house to reject these bills, I am invoking, not only religious, but also social grounds.
I appeal to all those who love their country, who wish it to be great and strong, whatever their political or sectarian affiliations might be.
In the words of Paul Gide, a sincere Protestant: "Divorce is only a form of polygamy by instalments." Man does not mate, he marries, and when he marries, it is unto death.
tMr. Winkler.]
Marriage is not an ordinary contract, strictly natural or civil in character. The church intervenes to give it a much more august character. Husband and wife are united in the name of the Creator of mankind and their union is consecrated forevermore.
All moralists agree on the principle that the idea of perpetuity linked to duty makes the latter easier to accomplish. When you let a man realize that he may cast off his obligations, you weaken his sense of duty.
Monsignor Freppel stated in the French chamber of deputies on June 13, 1882:
Such is, gentlemen, the undeniable danger of divorce. With the possibility of breaking the bonds of matrimony, you introduce in the home a germ of dissolution, and what would be sufficient to develop this germ of dissolution? Any of the thousand and one annoyances which always arise when two people live together would be enough. When marriage is considered indissoluble, such annoyances may disappear sooner or later at the thought of a perpetual bond; hurt pride bows to reason and the idea of sacrifice finally triumphs over selfishness.
On the contrary, with the prospect of a complete and final breaking off everything is magnified, everything gets worse; the least disagreement takes on considerable importance. And the fatal word of divorce which civil law itself drops into the ear of this worker or that farmer, who would never have thought of it without this trap set against his frailty by the legislator himself, that word received apprehensively at first but which gradually sinks in, that word with which one gets familiar becomes the signal for a permanent dissolution of family life!
We must revert to the fundamental laws of marriage.
As Monsignor Julien put it during a lecture delivered at the Semaines sociales of France, in Grenoble, in 1923:
The question is whether the laws of the spirit will prevail over the laws of the flesh in the struggle for duty.
The question is whether the soul will remain faithful to duty to the extent of accepting its responsibilities, which are sometimes very heavy, and of running risks, which are at times very distressing. No prerogative, either legal or political, no reward, either in the form of money or of honours, will ever replace that which can only assure the fecundity of our families, namely, the respect for God-established order and the joy that springs from self-denial. It is the family spirit, if we may say so, that overcomes difficulties, the fears of the present and the uncertainties of the future, and that enables one to live up to the divine laws of life according to the dictates of one's conscience.
The family spirit, however, is properly the religious spirit. Religion is the best safeguard for this superior instinct which draws the sap of life to all the limbs of the human tree.
One may not sever with impunity the roots by which human institutions extend into the realm of divinity.

Mr. P. Cuche, professor at the Faculty of Law of Grenoble, states, with Monsignor Julien:
It is an acknowledged fact today that the mandatory effect of contracts does not lie in the will of the contracting parties. The fact that I wanted something yesterday does not imply that I still want it today. Even if I change my mind, I am still bound by my undertaking of yesterday. My agreement of yesterday thus prevails over my wish today, so that even though I change my mind I am still bound by this agreement.
Public interest requires that it be so. It is essential that the undertakings agreed to in marriage, a sacred contract, be permanent.
Man is not born to indulge in pleasure; he is born to do his duty, to live, to toil by the sweat of his brow, to fight weather and the elements in order to earn his living, to practise religion and charity, and so on.
Divorce breeds free love. We must therefore choose between indissoluble marriage and free love.
If we allow exceptions, they will soon become the rule.
Our legislation should respect and safeguard the family, the basis of society.
As long as by civil legislation the stability of our homes is left to the good will or whims, the egotism or passion of either of the parties concerned, the family as an institution will remain precarious because the two main objects of marriage, procreation and education of children and mutual assistance of the spouses, will be jeopardized.
The unity of the family and the indissolubility of marriage are characteristic of progressive civilizations; divorce means decline and retrogression.
It is the responsibility of the civil authority to legislate on the civil and temporal effects of marriage, but it has not the power to bind and even less to untie the bonds of matrimony.
The function of the state is to look after the general welfare of the community and the legislators have the duty to vigorously oppose every application for divorce. As I said at the outset, we are not qualified to hear those cases; if we persist in doing so, we usurp a right which belongs only to God.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).
He said: The purpose of this bill is to abolish capital punishment in Canada and to substitute therefor life imprisonment. May I state initially that I speak as a private member and not necessarily on behalf of my party. I hope that this contentious matter may remain out of the realm of party politics.
Some hon. members may question the wisdom or desirability of such a bill at the present time. I suppose such an attitude is natural, because after two world wars in which millions of people were slain, where whole populations were wiped out, and in which we witnessed such incidents as Hiroshima and Nagasaki, some may feel that it is not very important whether a few worthless human beings, who have themselves taken human life, live or die. I feel, however, that this Canadian law is so revolting that parliament should examine it before another session goes by. At least twice before similar legislation has been before parliament. In 1914 and again in 1917 Mr. Robert Bickerdike, the member for Montreal-St. Lawrence, introduced such a bill. Unfortunately he did not get very far with it.
Then in 1937 a Mr. Blair introduced a bill which would have substituted for hanging a more humane method of execution. That proposal also was not accepted. Thus in 1950 we still have hanging on the statute books of Canada. Surely the time has come for reform. Few members can study this issue without realizing that there are very grave

Criviinal Code Amendvient objections to the death penalty. I do not think I am sentimental about this subject. Certainly I am going to try to base my arguments on other than sentimental reasons. I believe that any criminal should be punished and punished adequately, but I also believe that there are sound and logical reasons why Canada should do away with the death penalty.
I have seven main reasons for objecting to hanging. My first reason is based upon purely moral and Christian grounds. Most Canadians profess to believe in the Christian faith. That faith is based at least partly upon the ten commandments. Most hon. members will recall the words of the sixth commandment, and those words are specific, concise and crystal clear. They are, "Thou shalt not kill". There are no ifs, there are no buts, there are no qualifications. I submit that if that commandment means anything at all, it means exactly what it says: "Thou shalt not kill."
But in Canada we have moved an amendment to that commandment and we have said in effect "the state may kill, but the individual must not take a life".

speechtext: An eye for an eye.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
I say that if it is wrong for an individual to kill, it is equally wrong for the state to take a human life. I do not profess to be a biblical authority like my hon. friend the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair). I am not going to quote citations from the Bible tonight to back up my argument, but I say that hanging violates every Christian principle. If we expect the individual to refrain from murder, the state must set an example. Perhaps I do not see this matter in the proper light, but as I do see it, no Christian can advocate capital punishment and be true to his faith, and no community which professes to be Christian can deliberately murder even the most erring of its members.
My second objection to hanging is the terrible brutality of the actual execution. In 1937 some shocking evidence was placed before a select committee of this House of Commons. Some hon. members may not have read the evidence. Many experts claim that hanging is almost instantaneous, that death comes instantly. According to the evidence presented to that select committee that is not correct. At page 57 of the evidence Mr. S. Wills, acting deputy sheriff of the city of Toronto, testified that in eleven hangings from 1917 to 1937 which he had attended the average time of death after the trap was


sprung was 14-7 minutes. At page 55 he was asked by Mr. Howden about a specific case, and I quote:
Q. Was death fairly rapid in that instance?
A. There has not been one rapid one that I have seen yet.
According to the Toronto deputy sheriff mishaps are quite common at executions. At page 53 he stated:
I have always had at the back of my mind1 the possibility of decapitation every time there is a hanging. There is always the fear of that.
Such a fear apparently is well justified because there are numerous instances of mishaps having taken place in Canadian executions. One of them was mentioned in this evidence, the caset of a woman in Montreal who had her head literally pulled off in the execution. The following is in the evidence:
Q. Did the woman's friends see her after her head was pulled off?
A. That I could not say.
Other accidents have taken place in Canadian executions. On page 54 of the evidence Mr. Hamilton questioned the Toronto deputy sheriff as follows:
Q. Have there been any bunglings by the executioner in the eleven cases you have mentioned?
A. Well, I have one case in mind where a man was allowed to have too long a drop, and on going down to the lower cell, I found that the man was practically on his knees when he got down at the end of the rope . . . the hangman had gotten down before me, and I found him hanging onto the man so as to ensure his speedy death.
Q. You mean to say that he was pushing down on the man?
A. Yes, sir, hanging on to the man with his weight to bring him on to the rope until he was dead.
I suggest that hon. members should read this evidence, because there are numerous cases just as shocking as those I have mentioned. I say hanging is inhuman. It is unChristian. It is a foul practice which has no place in a civilized country like Canada.
In the third place I am opposed to capital punishment because of its relentless finality. Once the punishment has been inflicted there is no possible rectification in case of error. It is human to err; judges and juries can and do make mistakes. No matter how careful juries may be, no matter how damning the evidence may appear, it is possible to hang an innocent man; and history recounts numerous instances where that has been done. Before the British house a few years ago Sir Fitzroy Kelly declared that from the turn of the century to 1930 he had found seventeen cases in Britain of accused men having been sentenced to death and subsequently found to be innocent. I say that such a danger is always present; and until human judgment is

infallible I doubt if we have the right to inflict irrevocable doom upon any of our fellow citizens.
Capital punishment brutalizes and degrades every person associated with it, the guards who lead the victim to the gallows, the executioner who must spring the trap door. I have heard some interesting stories about some of these executioners, and I am sure some of them must be true. Some executioners commit suicide because of their job. I know that one executioner in one of our large cities not so long ago was a consistent drunkard. At one time an execution was to take place in that city. The deputy sheriff is responsible; and as the date of the execution approached the authorities could not find the hangman. The sheriff was ready to resign rather than be responsible for springing the trap door. Finally they found the hangman; but not before the prison official had been thoroughly frightened. I say capital punishment is hard upon the minister or priest who has to administer the last rites of the church, upon the doctor who has to be present, upon the reporters who have to write about it. The family of the man hanged have a terrible stigma cast upon them. One of the men hanged in Edmonton last month had five children; one of the men hanged in Vancouver had four. Even the people who read about hangings are affected by the inevitable horror; and I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that every execution is followed by a general lowering of the moral standards of a community. Hanging does not in any way enhance the majesty of Canadian law. I do not see how we can inculcate a respect for human life by ourselves showing contempt for human life.
My fifth reason for opposing the death penalty, and I think it is an important reason, is the fact that it is so repugnant to many decent citizens that the jurymen in capital cases have been known to bring in verdicts contrary to the evidence, in favour of a prisoner. Acquittals sometimes can be blamed only upon the humanitarian feelings of the jurymen and their reluctance to send a man to certain death. Many juries are reluctant to find a woman guilty of murder. Such verdicts, even if they occur but rarely, could be dangerous to a community, because of the fact that as a result dangerous criminals may be set free.
In the sixth place I oppose capital punishment because quite frequently Canadians are hanged who do not directly commit murder. Under Canadian law accessories to a murder are just as guilty as the man who committed the fatal act. In certain circumstances, for instance if a murder is committed during a
Criminal Code Amendment robbery, all those who participated in the robbery may be executed; and that has frequently happened in Canadian legal history. Some hon. members may remember the Bank of Hochelaga case in Montreal some years ago. If my memory serves me correctly in that case five men held up a bank and during the hold-up one of the robbers killed a bank employee. All five were subsequently executed for murder.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend has a point; that was a bad case. Yet some Canadians who have been killed in these mass executions have been young. Some have been veterans. We must remember that for five long years we taught a great many of our young men how to kill. We showed them the most gruesome, the most fiendish, the most scientific methods of murder. Can we be surprised if some do not forget those teachings overnight? I repeat that this law is one of which we may not be too proud.
Finally, I oppose the death penalty because as a punishment it is purely and simply revenge. No attempt is made to reform the criminal, nor is any attempt made to remove the conditions which led that man to become a murderer. I think-and I say this respectfully-that if we Canadians spent more time in eliminating those conditions which cause murders, and less time in brutal punishment after murders are committed, we might have a lower murder rate.
I have said that there are grave objections to the death penalty. Are there, then, logical reasons for Canada to continue it? What are the arguments for its retention? There are several arguments, some minor and one at least major. The first minor argument in favour of capital punishment goes something like this. Hanging removes the possibility of. a repetition of the crime of murder by the same offender. Of course

Criminal Code Amendment it does. But I also suggest that life imprisonment would do the same thing, and without compounding the crime of murder.
Some will say that life imprisonment is a burdensome expense upon the state, that there is no reason why the taxpayers should maintain a prisoner. That is not a very strong reason. In the first place, of course, most prisoners, after having been imprisoned for some time, should have acquired a trade by which to maintain themselves. If that is not the case in Canada then perhaps our penitentiaries should be examined to find out why that is not so. Moreover, I do not think most Canadians would be so selfish as to want to take the life of a man, simply to save the taxpayers a few cents a day on a per capita basis.
Such reasons are not good enough. In my opinion the sole justification for the retention of the death penalty in Canada, if there is any justification at all, is the argument that hanging discourages an a deters potential murderers. Many who believe in hanging frankly confess that it is a horrible and revolting practice, but they say it is necessary in order to protect society. Capital punishment, they argue, is a necessary deterrent without which there would be more murders. Well, if such a claim were justified I would admit that it would be a pretty strong argument; but history gives little support to the theory that hanging is a deterrent to crime.
The experience of the English people is noteworthy, and I should like to draw that experience to the attention of the house. It may surprise some hon. members to learn that until a century or so ago English common law was perhaps as harsh as any law in the civilized world, and capital punishment was carried out in the British isles on a colossal scale.
In 1780 there were 240 capital crimes in Great Britain. In those days you could be hanged for picking pockets, for fishing on the estate of a lord or for hunting on his grounds. There were thousands of trivial crimes punishable by hanging. During the reign of Henry VIII 72,000 Englishmen were hanged, and most of them for trivial offences. The gruesome corpses were left hanging along country roads to serve as grim warnings to potential evildoers.
Despite this terrible severity, crime in England steadily increased. Hanging did not seem to deter it. All of these barbarous punishments in the past were justified by the excuse that hanging was necessary in order to deter further crime, the same excuse which is given today for retaining hanging for murder. Gradually down through the years
[Mr. Thatcher.l
men became a little kindlier, and a little more imaginative. The crimes punishable by death were gradually reduced in number. But they were not reduced without a great deal of opposition in the House of Lords and the House of Commons.
In 1810, for instance, Sir Samuel Romilly moved a bill in the English House of Commons to abolish capital punishment for theft to the value of five shillings and upwards. At that time the solicitor general stated:
All the judges of the land are convinced that the proposed reform is fraught with consequences the most injurious . . .
That was a statement by the solicitor general, a cabinet minister. Lord Ellen-borough, the famous chief justice, stated:
Repeal this law, and no man can trust himself for an hour out of doors . . . lest his property will be swept off by the hardened robber.
In those days many wise and learned men were aghast at the proposed reform. They said that no one's property would be safe if hanging were abolished for that trivial crime. Today we know their fears were groundless, and the prophecies concerning the increase of crime were completely falsified by subsequent history.
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that only a few centuries ago there was hardly a responsible person in Europe who did not think that the safety of the state depended upon its right to hang others who practised their religion in the wrong way. Not many centuries ago if you happened to live in France or Spain, you might have been hanged for being a Protestant. If you happened to live in England or Holland, you might have been hanged for being a Catholic. Despite that fact we know that religion flourished in most of the countries in Enurope.
I stated a moment ago that England has used capital punishment more extensively than any other country in the world. It is interesting to note what the English have done about capital punishment during the last fifteen years. Three times the House of Commons has passed a bill abolishing the death penalty, and three times the House of Lords, a non-elected body, has vetoed the bill.
If we abolish hanging in Canada, it is fair to ask whether it would be dangerous to our citizens generally. I say it would not be dangerous if we can go by the experience of other nations. In the world today there are more than thirty nations and states who have had experience with the abolition of capital punishment. In Europe such nations as Holland, Belgium, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Switzerland and others have dispensed with the death penalty. In North and

South America it has been abolished by such countries as the Argentine, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Uruguay.
Back in 1930 the British House of Commons set up a select committee to inquire into the question of capital punishment. This committee wrote to the foreign countries who had abolished capital punishment requesting them to send in evidence. The committee asked: "Tell us what your experience was before you abolished the death penalty, and what your experience was afterwards; did the murder rate go up?" They also invited those countries to send qualified experts, whose passage to England would be paid, to testify before the committee. The evidence which was given to that British committee in 1930 was so enlightening that I should like to put some of it on Hansard for the benefit of members, so that they might ponder it.
In Belgium there have been no executions since 1863. The Belgian attitude to the death penalty was summed up in a memorandum sent to the committee by the minister of justice. I quote from that memorandum:
Since the death penalty was definitely abandoned the crime ratio has remained practically stationary . . .
In the face of results so conclusive .... it seems inconceivable that a minister of justice should ever again think it possible to re-establish a penalty the uselessness of which has been amply demonstrated.
In Denmark the last execution took place in 1892. The Danish minister of justice stated to the committee:
It may be considered proved that the abolition of this punishment has not had any adverse influence on the number of capital crimes.
Mr. Erik Kampmann, representing the Danish government, told the select committee:
The number of murders decreased since the virtual abolition of the death penalty.
In Holland capital punishment was abolished by law in 1870. Today its homicide rate is the lowest on the continent of Europe.
Representing his government, Sir Simon Van Der Aa was a witness before this committee on capital punishment. He stated that following abolition-
-criminal statistics continued to show no tendency of increase of crimes for which, in lieu of the death penalty, lifelong imprisonment may be imposed.
In Norway there have been no executions since 1875-that is, there had not been until the war. According to official statistics, the annual murder rate per 100,000 has been as follows: 1859-1868, -17; 1869-1870, -14; 18791888, -12; 1889-1898, -12; 1899-1904, 08; 19051924, -05. It has dropped consistently. In a memorandum to the select committee, the Norwegian government stated:
The experience gained has strengthened the view that abolition of capital punishment has not caused any increase in the number of murders.
Criminal Code Amendment
Sweden abolished the death penalty in 1921, although the last execution was in 1910. In a report to the committee, the chief of Swedish penitentiaries said:
The final abolition of the penalty far from leading to an increase in offences of this kind was actually followed by a noticeable decrease in crimes legally punished by death.
Mr. Speaker, one could go on to show that every country which gave evidence before the British committee testified that the murder rate, if not remaining stationary, had actually gone down. In no single instance is there evidence of the murder rate having increased after the abolition of the death penalty.
Several states in the union to the south of us have also abolished the death penalty. The murder rate is high in many of the states, but it is a matter of statistics that the murder rate in those states which have abolished capital punishment is lower than in those in which there is some form of execution. There may be a reason for that; I do not know. But I say that the experience of the foreign countries, and the experience of some of the American states, proves that the murder rate does not necessarily go up when the death penalty is removed.
There is one final reason, Mr. Speaker, why I do not believe execution is a deterrent to crime. Most murders take place in moments of great passion. They are caused by rage, fear, jealousy, drink, insanity or something of that nature. At the moment the murder is committed, the murderer is usually so blinded by his passion of the moment and his unreasoning fury that no thought of future punishment ever enters his mind until later. I say that over these influences no deterrent can have very great effect. No matter how hon. members wish to approach this problem, I suggest it is almost impossible to prove that the death penalty is a deterrent to murder. I challenge any member of parliament to name one person who can be proven to have been deterred from murder because of his fear of the consequences to himself. This being the case, it seems to me that the only possible justification for keeping the death penalty is based upon fallacious reasoning.
Is there a satisfactory alternative to the death penalty? I think there is. I believe that life imprisonment would be a satisfactory alternative. I believe such a punishment should be exactly what its name implies, imprisonment for life. It would punish effectively. It is a deterrent; it removes the criminal from society, and allows for the reformation of the individual. In addition to that, it recognizes the sanctity of human life. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that real security for human life is to be found in reverence

Criminal Code Amendment for it. If the law regarded it as inviolable, then people would also begin to regard it in that light. Perhaps I am biased on this subject, but I cannot believe that there is one single admissible argument in favour of the retention of the death penalty. I say that a humanitarian age places the burden of proof upon those who would retain the death penalty, not on those who would abolish it. As a society, we have always believed that life should be protected and preserved; and I suggest that we put that practice into our penal code.
Not so long ago a hundred crimes were punishable by death, then fifty, then twenty and finally one. I suggest tonight that we make the record clean. I suggest that we in this parliament prove that we are civilized enough, and morally developed enough to let this vileness disappear from our Criminal Code for all time. Surely the world is tragic enough. These ghastly human sacrifices every so often in the Dominion of Canada are no credit to our nation. I feel for the Solicitor General who, I understand, is the man who from time to time must decide whether an appeal can be granted or whether it cannot. It is a task that I would not want, and I do not envy him his responsibility. Perhaps. this bill will not pass this session, perhaps it will not pass at the next; but, Mr. Speaker, sooner or later it will pass because this is a bill which modern civilization will demand. If this bill does not pass this session, I shall re-introduce it next session and if necessary I shall re-introduce it at the one thereafter. I commend this bill to the serious consideration of all hon. members. If they study it, I think they will find some merit in it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
The proposed bill, Mr. Speaker, seeks to amend section 263 of the Criminal Code, punishment for the crime of murder by providing, instead of the sentence of death, imprisonment for life; and under section 299, for the crime of rape, by making the same provision. It does not seek to remove the death penalty under section 74 for treason, under which section there are eleven subheadings as to what constitutes treason. It does not remove the death penalty under section 137 relating to piracy.
Under section 250, homicide is defined as the killing of a human being by another, directly or indirectly, by any means whatsoever; and it may be either culpable or not culpable as defined in section 252 of the Canadian Criminal Code; and other definitions are contained in sections 253 to 257 inclusive. The proposed amendment also seeks to remove the death penalty for rape. I do not think this house will be much concerned with that, as the statistics I have procured from the department show that from 1928 to 1948


inclusive there were 463 convictions for rape in Canada, and nobody was hanged as a result of those convictions.
Under section 261 of the Criminal Code culpable homicide may be reduced to manslaughter if death comes in the heat of passion caused by sudden provocation. The previous speaker mentioned that a great many of the crimes resulting in murder were the result of the heat of passion. Such is not the case. If they were, Mr. Speaker, as you are well aware, the sentence can be commuted and it invariably has been commuted in Canada. As a matter of fact, the figures show that the crime of murder in Canada has decreased in the last ten years as compared with the preceding ten years, and that the major crimes of murder in Canada are associated with robbery with violence where the crime was absolutely thought out and prepared ahead of time; they were not done in the heat of passion. The last case that we had on the records in our courts down in Quebec was a case of premeditated murder where the innocent passengers of a plane were all sent to their death by a man who thought the thing out carefully and procured the bomb.
This matter has been dealt with in this house on many occasions. It was brought before the house by a former member. My hon. friend who has just spoken says he is going to bring the matter before the house next session, the session after that and the session after that. I presume he will be through the session after that, so we shall have it brought before the house three times. But there was a member of this house who brought the matter up many times prior to the year 1921. He brought it up session after session. In 1919 Mr. Mowat, the then member for Parkdale, moved to amend the section of the code by providing for electrocution instead of hanging. That is covered in Hansard at page 148, volume I, of the 1919 session. At page 488 of the same volume of Hansard the then member for Renfrew South, Mr. Pedlow, moved an amendment as follows:
The death penalty is abolished and all crimes heretofore punishable by death shall be punishable by an incarceration not to exceed the remainder of the life of the accused.
In that debate it is interesting to note that Mr. A. Thompson, the then member for Yukon Territory, adjoining the United States territory of Alaska, said:
In his country, perhaps, but it does not in the Yukon Territory. We have hanged every man that ever committed a murder: we hanged him quick and it has had a very deterrent effect upon other would-be murderers ... in Alaska life is held cheap by the criminal class as compared with the way it is regarded by the same class in the Yukon Territory.

That is the way the two territories, one governed by the United States and one governed by ourselves, operated the death penalty on a different basis. The matter never came to a vote in that session. In 1923 Mr. William Irvine, the then member for Calgary East, formerly Social Credit and later C.C.F., moved a bill to amend the Criminal Code by repealing all provisions thereof demanding capital punishment and the substitution of life imprisonment for the death sentence. He quoted from the book by the warden of Sing Sing, Warden Lawes, at page 1270, that out of 85 men who committed homicide in American states where capital punishment was in effect only one was actually executed, and in the cases where the future consequences entered into the calculations of the convict when he committed the crime, he resolved himself as almost certain to be one of the 84 who would escape death. Apparently it has not been a deterrent in those states where it has been abolished.
I contend that the punishment is inflicted as an end to maintain public peace, good order and morality, and out of respect to the laws and regulations which are the cornerstone of our social relations. We are the lawmakers here in this house and have a responsibility to the public, regardless of our personal abhorrence of hanging. None of us like the matter of hanging. The intervention of the lawmaker-and we are that-is not only legitimate but also absolutely necessary, and he has the right also to punish. He punishes to prevent the repetition of misdemeanors like those which have been committed, such as murder; and the lawmaker's acts are accordingly beneficial to the country at large, and that is our special social mission. Murder cannot be recognized with leniency and maudlin sentiment if every right-thinking man and woman wishes that the temple of society shall' remain standing and desires that civic and constitutional liberties now enjoyed shall continue.
Up until 1924, when that debate took place, Mr. De Quiros in his book "Modern Theories of Criminality" referred to a table giving the ratio of homicides of all degrees, for every million inhabitants. My hon. friend who has spoken mentioned Belgium and some of the other countries. You will find that in Mexico, for instance, there were one thousand murders per million of population, and there is no hanging there. In Chile the number of murders was 340 per million of population; in the Argentine, 230 per million; in the United States of America, 120 per million, and so on; while in Canada the number is only 2-6 per million of population.
Criminal Code Amendment
It will be noted that Canada was the lowest despite the fact that about that time about one-half of our ratio of homicides were committed by people of foreign countries who had come to Canada.
We have the lowest figure of homicides in the world. It is to be noted that life imprisonment does not mean always what its words imply. The crown always has the right to revise a sentence and has done so, reducing it on some occasions to 10 years and in one case as low as 2 years. I would point out too the safeguards that a man accused of murder has, namely: one, the right to obtain counsel, and if he has not the money to do so the crown will appoint and pay counsel for him; two, counsel has the right to challenge 24 jurymen peremptorily, and 12 jurymen being selected, 36 people can be chosen from by counsel for the accused. If he calls no evidence he has the right to address the jury after the crown counsel. Even after a finding of guilty and a sentence of death, he has the right to apply to the governor in council for remission of the sentence of hanging to that of imprisonment. The whole evidence is reviewed by the Minister of Justice and the assistants in his department, who check not only the evidence given in the court below but all exhibits and any recommendations made by the jury or the trial judge. The accused in addition in the trial always has the benefit of the judge's charge to the jury, that if they have a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused it is their sworn duty to give the benefit of that doubt to the accused. In the cases of those under 18 years of age, even despite sentence of hanging being imposed, no sentences have been carried out.
It is interesting to note the number of commutations in Canada after a sentence of hanging for murder has been imposed. I have all the figures here. They show that the sentences of more people for hanging were commuted than actual hangings that have taken place. As I pointed out, in the last ten years hangings for murder in Canada have decreased considerably over the previous ten years. I submit with respect that we in this legislature should rely not only on our own judgment in these things but on the judgment of other lawyers and preservers of the peace who have given consideration to this matter in previous debates in the house.
In speaking in the debate, the late respected Ernest Lapointe, minister of justice, at page 1285 of Hansard, volume 2, 1924, quoted the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, home secretary of Great Britain, when dealing with a deputation from societies seeking the abolition of the death penalty in England, as follows:
He pointed out, however, that any government must take public opinion into account, and that so

Criminal Code Amendment far as his long parliamentary experience went there was little evidence of any general public desire for abolition, the subject not having been debated for many years. He also pointed out that before a government could recommend an alteration in that law they would have to consider very carefully what satisfactory alternative punishment they could properly suggest.
Mr. Lapointe gave his opinion as follows:
I am in the same position in this country, and I must share the views of Mr. Henderson. As far as my own personal feelings are concerned, by temperament and by instinct I would be inclined to vote for the bill, but from a high sense of duty I feel that I cannot do so, and that for the present we must retain capital punishment. H I were convinced that any other form of punishment would be as effective for the protection of the Canadian people, it would be my duty to recommend its adoption. It is because I do not believe that capital punishment can be replaced by any other form of punishment which would be as effective that I am forced to take this stand.
That was the opinion of a very eminent Canadian. In addition, there is the opinion of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in the same debate, who expressed similar views. He also stated that, in his opinion, hanging did act as a definite deterrent on the commission of the crime of murder. The argument can be used, and has been used by the hon. member who preceded me, that in one, two or three cases the actual hanging was not done in a very workmanlike manner. But these are exceptional cases. He will find that is true if he checks over the debates that have taken place in this house, because they went thoroughly into that matter.
In the same debate at page 1297 of Hansard the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, former prime minister, said:
If I believed that the bill which the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) has introduced would make for the preservation of innocent human life, would make in the end for a greater saving of human life, as is his object in proposing to substitute a sentence for life instead of the death penalty, I would vote with him. But I believe to the contrary; I believe that the deterrent effect of the death penalty, having regard to human society as it is constituted and to human character as we know it, is in the end to protect innocent people from the murderous assaults that may be made upon them by some of the individuals who compose our human society.
I believe that the death penalty does Jiave a deterrent effect, and I feel that more strongly because of the knowledge I have of the number of capital cases that have come before the cabinet in the short time in which this government has been in office, where we have had before us the circumstances of every individual case of murder that has taken place. These cases have revealed clearly the fact that the men who have been found guilty of murder have premeditated the crime for the most part from motives of lust or avarice. Were they and others like them to suffer only life imprisonment for their crimes, knowing the psychological effect exercised upon other minds and natures when such crimes are committed, I believe that the number of murders would vastly increase once the death penalty were abolished.

In addition, the argument has been used that if we dispense with the death penalty people will do as they have done in the southern states, namely, invoke the unwritten law and start to lynch. I have not very much fear of Canadians following that course. However, that is an argument that has been used against the abolition of the death penalty.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Nine o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
I would say further that if you pass the amendment you will in effect be saying:	No matter how dastardly
the crime, no matter how long he may have premeditated it, he could offend against society with impunity, knowing he would not have to face the death penalty of hanging. In cases which have been occurring with frequency, such as men entering homes, store premises and banks, with gun in hand, killing old age pensioners for their cheques, young bank tellers, aged storekeepers, surely these men who deliberately and premeditatedly kill have placed themselves beyond the pale of human sympathy, and we should be concerned, not with sympathy for them, but with sympathy for the thousands of men, women and children throughout the land whose lives are in our keeping. Human life is getting too cheap in Canada at the hands of armed thugs, and the thing for us to do is to maintain the supreme punishment.
It is idle to ask: Where are your statistics as to whether hanging deters murderers? It seems to me that any lawyer who is handling cases and is not, through long practice, entirely prejudiced in favour of the accused, knows that hanging is a deterrent. Every soldier who served overseas knows that a certain law of death for desertion was a deterrent. Every individual Canadian citizen knows that the ignominious death by hanging is a deterrent and that people who through passion, drunkenness or otherwise are inclined to carry on on many occasions are deterred in their own minds by threat of the sentence of hanging by the neck. If they knew that all they could suffer was a term of imprisonment which might be shortened by the assistance of friends and those people who will always sign a petition, is it not logical to assume that some of them at least would commit the crime if this deterrent were removed?

I am just about through. You are inviting them to do so and you will be responsible for the death of more innocent people. Yours will be the responsibility and I for one do not intend to assume it. We owe protection to the public and a sentence of hanging is the protection to

innocent men, women and children. It should be noted that when a vote was taken in 1924 on a similar bill it was defeated 92 to 29. Another bill was introduced later on and was again defeated in the house. There are other lengthy quotations I could give from the late R. B. Bennett, who was also against the abolition of capital punishment.
Some of us have defended men charged with murder and have been rather successful in saving a lot of rope, according to the mounted police. Some of us are able to say that none of our clients was ever hanged, although perhaps the public have thought that they should have been. In England the House of Lords refused to abolish capital punishment and we in Canada should be most careful before we remove this protection for innocent men, women and children from some thugs on the street who are ready to commit premeditated murder with a gun. I am against the bill.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bradley for the appointment of a special committee to consider and suggest amendments to the Dominion Elections Act.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we rose for the dinner recess I had expressed a desire to add a few words to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) who had stressed the desirability of revising the rules governing the recording of the votes of servicemen. During the last election servicemen across Canada were permitted to record their choice of candidates in the various constituencies, whether they were serving in one of His Majesty's Canadian ships or in one of the various stations of the army or air force.
According to the reports which have been received since the general election, and particularly in view of the evidence produced at an inquiry held into the election of a member in Nova Scotia, it is quite evident that there was much misunderstanding by those charged with the responsibility of recording votes and by those who wanted to cast votes for particular candidates. The report of the commissioners to be found on page 80 of Votes and Proceedings contains these words:
The officers in charge seem to have had little conception of the importance of their duties and the necessity of strictly carrying out the regula-
Dominion Elections Act tions. Matters were not improved by a "signal" from air force headquarters which the officer interpreted to mean that he was to make no inquiry as to the qualification of voters and that once an envelope was presented to him with a signature, he was to give the holder a ballot even if he knew that the person was not entitled to vote.
I do not think it is unreasonable to expect that there would be considerable anxiety or indifference or disagreement in connection with the methods by which the servicemen were to cast their votes. It is not customary in the services to discuss politics or the various doctrines advanced by political parties or the methods by which candidates are elected. I think the officers of the services have complete justification for pleading ignorance of the details of carrying out an election. Therefore if the responsibility for the recording of votes can be removed from the commanding officers to officials of the chief electoral officer, so much the better.
I should like to call attention to one phrase in the paragraph I have quoted where reference is made to the envelope being presented with a signature. That caused a great deal of uncertainty in the minds of service voters. When a man entered a polling booth established in the company office or the training centre or the ship, he was presented with an envelope upon which was written the name of the voter. The man recorded his vote for the candidate in his particular constituency, placed his ballot in the envelope which was sealed in his presence, and the envelope was then dispatched to some central headquarters where it was opened before a returning officer and such scrutineers as might be appointed.
Personally I believe that everything was aboveboard, but in the mind of the serviceman there was always the doubt as to whether the manner in which he had recorded his vote might not have been noticed and recorded because of his having signed his name on the envelope. I do not think he blamed his own officer but he had the idea that somewhere along the chain an opportunity would be afforded to some unknown individual to open the envelope and see how he had voted. I am quite prepared to admit that those doubts were quite unjustified, but they still remained in the mind of the ordinary serviceman. He felt that he was not being given the privilege of a secret ballot, that an opportunity was being afforded to someone in the Department of National Defence or elsewhere in the government service to open that envelope and see how he had recorded his vote.
An opportunity is now being given to revise the system of recording the servicemen's votes. I hope that this committee will review

Dominion Elections Act the system so that the serviceman may feel that he has the same privilege as any other Canadian citizen of recording his vote secretly so that nobody, either directly or indirectly connected with him, may be able to ascertain how he has cast his vote. This is one of the main things the committee should inquire into when reviewing amendments to the elections act.
There is another point I should like to raise, and that is regarding fishermen. The fishermen are given the opportunity of recording their votes at advanced polls, but I understand that these polls were not established in all constituencies where there were a number of fishermen. The result was that a fisherman going to sea on his lawful business and expecting to be away on election day could not record his vote in his own constituency; he had to go to a neighbouring constituency.
I take this opportunity of bringing these two points to the attention of the committee in the hope that they will review them and see whether amendments cannot be introduced to relieve the uncertainty in the mind of the serviceman and to give the fisherman the opportunity of recording his vote in his own constituency when it is necessary for him to be at sea to carry on his fishing [DOT] operations according to the season of the year.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to make certain observations with reference to the conduct of elections in general, and I think perhaps this is an appropriate time to do so. First of all I think it is advisable that our general election machinery and procedure for taking the expressed will of the people should be subject to such a review from time to time as this motion envisages. I thought the subject was debated on a rather broad basis this afternoon, and I should like to mention one thing which was said by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). I only do so because his judgment and views are highly respected in the house, and I would not mention my disagreement with him if it were not for the high respect in which his views are held. I do not like his suggestion of Americanizing our way of holding elections.
I realize there may be advantages in the suggestion he has made of regular general elections, but I think such advantages are overruled, overbalanced and outweighed by the numerous advantages of the British system. It may be, as he says, that the dice are somewhat loaded in favour of a government, but after all we who have been in the opposition for a long time have perhaps become accustomed to certain things that are almost inherent in our system with respect to oppositions and governments. Even if the dice are
[Mr. Pearkes.l

a little loaded in favour of a government nevertheless I think a government ought to be given a certain amount of elasticity and non-rigidity in choosing the time when a general election is to be held, but of course within the statutory limits that are presently provided. Whenever a government feels that it should consult the people it does so at its own risk because if the people think they have been consulted too soon or too late they always have the democratic right of dealing with the government on that point in addition to others.
I should not like to see this country come to the position where an election would have to be held on a definite date fixed for every four or five years and everybody aware of that date for years ahead. I should like to see the present system continued. I have great difficulty, Mr. Speaker, in competing with those who are talking over there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I should not like to see the committee deal with this matter in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Macleod. I believe there are advantages in our present system of leaving it in the hands of a government to decide when to go to the country, within certain statutory limitations. I believe if we departed from that system we would lose something so far as our democratic British principles are concerned, and I think we would feel the loss greatly. Even if some of us have been in opposition for a long time we are still prepared to allow the government to exercise that function because it is a part of our British system, and that must always be preserved.
There is another point I should like to mention. Although there may be instances here and there in the public life of Canada, and in some cases they may have been rather glaring, I think most members of the house who have been here for any length of time will agree with me that, taking a broad view of the whole political picture in Canada, Canadians conduct their elections in a pretty clean manner, and I doubt if any other part of the world does so any more cleanly than we do. We all have our weaknesses, but in my time in any event, so far as elections are concerned, I have no knowledge of anything other than thoughtless irregularities, and none of them have finally affected the ultimate results so far as the will of the people was concerned.
That does not mean we should rest upon our oars. I think it is the duty and responsibility of members of parliament to try to maintain as great a degree of purity in our election affairs as possible. In these days when people with other ideologies are trying to upset our

method of government and substitute therefor certain systems under which we would not have any election act as we understand it, I think it devolves upon us, and the responsibility becomes just that much heavier, to see that we try to conduct ourselves on a high plane in democratic elections in Canada and in other democratic states throughout the world.
I really wanted to mention two details which the committee in their wisdom might decide to deal with. One is the question of providing advance polls, as suggested by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). I think there are many of us who feel that there ought to be more provision for advance polls in our ridings. I am rather inclined to think that the act might be widened a little to take in others who are not presently included so far as the right to vote at an advance poll is concerned. It is rather limited in its application at the present time. Because of people having to travel, because of numbers of people living in places other than where they are working, it seems to me we might widen the provisions of the present act to allow certain other classes to vote at advance polls, and to try to arrange for such polls in every riding if at all possible.
I should like to make one other observation in that connection. In many ridings there are a great number of commuters, hundreds of whom use railway trains. In the House of Commons there must be at least thirty or thirty-five members, and perhaps more than that, who do not represent city ridings but ridings that are not too far away from cities, and the people in their constituencies are able to commute in and out to work. With our present hours of voting many good citizens are prevented from utilizing their franchise at all. In some instances in urban constituencies people are given two hours to vote, but so far as the commuter is concerned very often it means the loss of a whole day's work if he is going to vote at all. If he must travel by train for thirty, thirty-five or forty miles to get to his work he has to leave before the poll opens and cannot possibly return before it closes. So I think the committee ought to consider some provision whereby this very responsible section of our people may not be disfranchised by reason of any such obstacles put in their way,
Then I wanted to mention those who may be incapacitated by reason of illness at the time of an election. I know I am treading upon dangerous ground when I mention that subject, because if we were to open the door as wide as we might wish, having in mind some individual cases of which we have knowledge, we might find ourselves in the
Dominion Elections Act position of almost providing curb service for the people in connection with the exercise of their franchise. None of us would want to go anything like that far, I am sure; nevertheless where we have large numbers of people in hospitals and similar institutions, where the practical obstacles would not appear to be too great, I do believe we should provide some service which would permit them to record their votes. I am quite sure our hospital population on any given date would amount to a sizeable figure, and I do not think those people should have insult added to injury, if I may so express it, by not only suffering the inconvenience and pain of illness but by losing their franchise as well. I should like to see this committee discuss that matter and deal with it as they may see fit. I have no further suggestions to offer in that regard. I know many doubts will be expressed as to the practicability of such a proposal; nevertheless I believe the matter should be fully aired, and if there is some practical way by which it can be done then I think those of our people who are ill on election day should be given the opportunity of exercising their franchise in the normal way.
My last point is in connection with the polling of the maximum number of votes on election day. Members of parliament and men and women actively interested in the political realm generally wonder why people do not get out to vote in larger numbers; but of course all people are not as interested as members of parliament, candidates and those taking part in the work of an election. Very often when we have a particular interest we think everyone else should have the same interest. Unfortunately that is not the case, though a strong argument might be advanced that after all our people should have no greater interest than their interest in our democratic processes, and I subscribe to that argument. But I think we must recognize the public's position as well as our own. I remember a friend of mine, who did not belong to my political faith, once saying to me, "I cannot understand it. At a gathering the other night none of my friends knew anyone by name in the House of Commons except two cabinet ministers."

speechtext:
I think he mentioned the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and I took him for two. I replied, "I would not worry too much about that. The public cannot be expected to take an interest in everything; they have not time." I went on to ask him what church he belonged to, and he said the United Church. I said, "Well, you should be interested in your own church.

Dominion Elections Act Who is your moderator?" He replied, "By dads, I don't know. I knew the one ten years ago, but I have not known one since then." So I think we must not ask too much of the public; they are only human; but I do believe they should be encouraged and assisted to reach the polls on election day. A great many people never bother much about an election until it is almost upon them. Great numbers do not make any plans for going to the polling booths; many do not even bother to find out where they are until they go to vote. One thing that might be suggested by way of reform would be to show people where and when they vote. This perhaps would not be so essential in a rural constituency, but it is particularly important where the population is more heavily concentrated.
So I believe we might consider going back to the practice which once was followed, in my opinion with very good results; that is, the practice of sending postcards to the voters a week or less before the election, showing the place, date and hours of voting. Many candidates do this themselves in order to get the vote out. I have not done it, but I know of others who have gone to great expense in sending out postcards a few days before the election showing where the voters should go to cast their ballots; and I believe that is an outlay the government itself might well assume. Hon. members will recall that under the present legislation a copy of the voters' list for the particular subdivision must be sent to each qualified voter; and on that list the voter will see the place of polling, the date, and the hours. However, I am afraid we are all the same, and it is easy to lose a piece of paper even as large as that. Most people do not have a filing system or a filing clerk, and these things get mislaid. Another point is that these lists are sent out some two or three weeks before the election, though at the moment I have forgotten the exact time, since the revision has not taken place up to that time; and in the interval the whole business is often forgotten.
I am going to suggest to the committee that when they sit they might profitably consider leaving that voters' list provision as it is.
I think that is a good idea, because people can see whether someone else is on or off the list and the revision becomes that much simpler. I would not touch that provision, but I would add to what is already in the regulations the sending out of a card approximately a week before election day, notifying every qualified voter on the list where he or she should vote, the date of the polling, and the hours of polling. My judgment in this connection would perhaps be tempered by one consideration. If it were a tremendous
IMr. Graydon.]

expense to do this, then perhaps it would have to be considered in the light of the expenditure that would be incurred. Having regard to the importance that I attach, and which I fancy many members attach, to the desirability of getting as many people to the polls as possible on a voluntary basis, I suggest that this practice would be of inestimable value in seeing to it that the maximum number of qualified voters were at least shown the way to the polls.
I should like to make this suggestion in all good faith to the committee, in the hope that it will be considered. I am not a member of the committee, so for that reason I thought it wise to put the suggestion on the record. I should like to see this, and the numerous other matters which will come before that committee, thoroughly aired. In Canada we should try, as far as possible to have eventually the best machinery, and the cleanest, most decent system of electing members of parliament that is to be found in any democratic country in the world. It is a challenge which I think the people of Canada ought to accept.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the concluding remarks of the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) I am sure the whole house will be in full agreement. Several members have referred to the service vote, having particular reference to what took place at Greenwood. I feel it is desirable, and I think it is only fair to the services, that I should say a word of explanation.
At the outset I should like to express my appreciation to the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) for his fair, yes his generous, remarks about the services and their rather perplexing difficulties when face to face with the responsibility of carrying out a poll under service conditions. I thought both the remarks of the member for Nanaimo and the concluding remarks of the member for Peel illustrated that we are on the right track in setting up a committee to try to improve things if we can.
With regard to the service vote, everyone recognizes that service personnel are citizens. I happen to think they are very good citizens, and as such are entitled to vote. In the case of Greenwood there was no question but that all the service personnel who voted were entitled to vote somewhere. The only question was, were they entitled to vote at Greenwood where they cast their vote? And the question, of course, applies only to a minority of the men at Greenwood. I think hon. members who have taken the trouble to read the judges' report, or who have looked into the matter as carefully as I have through

no less than two sets of officers investigating the situation on the spot, will reach the conclusion that, while certainly votes were cast improperly at Greenwood, the improper casting of those votes was in no way due to any irregularities in the conduct of the polls, but was due to the fact that some of the men made a declaration of residence on the outside of the envelope which was not in accordance with the defence services voting regulations.

speechtext:
In Nova Scotia. Most of the service votes were quite properly cast there.
The explanation of how this arose is, I believe, simple, but is due to a rather complicated situation. Before the war there were no special regulations for taking the service vote; the ordinary civil procedure applied. In 1940 special regulations were adopted, and those were in effect in the general elections of 1940 and 1945. By and large, they gave satisfaction. I believe that no hon. member in this house will question the statement which I now make, that in the three general elections, 1940, 1945 and 1949, the way in which the service vote was taken showed a remarkable record of fairness.
At the conclusion of the war it was felt that the 1945 regulations required some additions to take care of the fact that service personnel would now be resident for considerable periods of time at stations which were at isolated centres. Accordingly when the election committee of this house was set up in 1947, the chief electoral officer put before that committee his recommendations as to the defence services voting regulations. The committee attached to its reports the text of the regulations as he had recommended them. Those are the regulations that are now in effect, letter by letter in accordance with the recommendations of the committee. The only change from the regulations previously in effect made in the regulations adopted in 1948, in consequence of the committee's report in 1947, was that the regulations of 1945 were amended by adding paragraph (b) to section 23 (1), to provide for service personnel having an option as to where they would vote. It is that option, made in consequence of the parliamentary committee's recommendation, which gave rise to the difficulty.
Those service electors who voted in the Annapolis-Kings election who were stationed at Greenwood voted in the place where they
Dominion Elections Act were ordinarily resident, as that term is used in reference to civilian electors in the election act. Had they been civilians, they would have been entitled to vote at Greenwood for whichever candidate they chose, but because of the special provision in the service regulations in order to vote at Greenwood they were required to make a declaration prior to January 1, 1949, almost six months before the election. It was something that few of them could be expected to do. This matter was called to their attention in orders, but still, in the nature of things, very few citizens will take some step six months before an election, before indeed the election is even announced, to put themselves in a position to vote. It was that requirement and that complication which gave rise to the difficulty.
I think hon. members will appreciate the fact that while the difficulty exists and has resulted in much misunderstanding, to use the words of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), and it is that misunderstanding which has given rise to this situation, it is by no means an easy matter to correct. It is by no means an easy matter to provide for a method of election which will enable service personnel situated at isolated centres, such as Shilo, Rivers, Goose Bay and a dozen other places across Canada, to exercise their franchise in the same way as an ordinary citizen would. Yet I believe it is desirable that, as far as possible, service personnel should exercise their franchise in the same way as the civilian.
The question was asked whether the committee would have the power to deal with this matter. Of course the committee has power to deal with everything having regard to the elections act. I may tell the members of the house that this is a matter that has been giving the officers of the Department of National Defence and the chief electoral officer a good deal of concern. They have been looking into the situation, examining how it is dealt with in other countries and trying to work out some suggestions that may be put before the committee for its consideration. But that is, I suggest, by no means easy. In any event, the committee and the house can be assured that in its work, with regard to both civilian voting and service voting, it will have the full co-operation of the officers concerned and of the officers of the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words, Mr. Speaker, before this motion carries. A good many suggestions have been made today which I hope the committee will consider. While I may not agree with all of them, it seems to me that many good points

Dominion Elections Act have been brought to the attention of the committee. There is just one that I would like to emphasize and perhaps I will go a little bit further than the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) went. I refer to the grievance that people feel when they are denied the right to vote because they have to be away from their home constituency on election day.
The hon. member for Peel made a useful suggestion when he proposed that the provision for voting at the advance poll should be widened somewhat. He suggested that the categories of people entitled to vote should be enlarged. I see no reason why there should be any limitation at all on the classes or categories of people entitled to vote at the advance poll. I know, for example, that in provincial elections in my own province of Manitoba it is possible for anyone who has to be away from his home constituency on election day to vote at the advance poll, simply by declaring that he has to be away.
Another possible solution of the problem might be found by taking a leaf from the book of British Columbia with respect to their practice in provincial elections. I understand that in that province there is quite an extensive arrangement for absentee voting. In other words, no matter where you are in the province of British Columbia on election day, you can cast your vote. If you are in your own constituency, you vote at your own poll. If you are out of your own constituency, you are permitted to vote wherever you are and to cast a ballot for the candidate of your choice back in your own constituency.
